name: Sam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at Granite Ridge, an open-cut coal mine. It's a machine the size of a house, the bucket takes about 50 tonnes a bite, and my job is to load the haul trucks as fast and clean as I can without wrecking the face. I'm the senior operator on our crew, so I train the new shovel operators and sort out problems with the dig plan. Good days are when the trucks never wait and the floor stays flat, bad days are when the cable gets run over or the ground is wet clay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The skill, I suppose. There's maybe four people at the mine who can dig a clean bench at full speed, and I'm one of them. My wife Helen runs a small hair salon in town, and she says I talk about the shovel the way other men talk about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, really. I'm not online much and people at work don't talk about AI, they talk about the roster and the price of coal. If someone asked, I'd say I never thought it'd come to much in a place like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I do. That's fine by me. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't feel I've missed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep running the shovel, keep training the new ones, keep the bit we put away each month going. Maybe replace the pickup next year like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's just a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the job in a normal year, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coal itself, more than computers. Every few years there's talk the mine's got fifteen years left, then ten. That's the thing that'd actually move us, not a chat program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine did start winding down, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the work, probably. There's a couple of other mines within two hours' drive. I wouldn't love the driving but I'd do it.

S0.say: I'd say not much, because people at work talk about the roster and the coal price, not AI. If asked, I'd say I never thought it'd come to much in a place like this.
S0.think: It means I keep doing what I do, and that's fine by me. I've never used an AI tool and I don't feel I've missed out.
S0.do: Keeps running the shovel and training new operators. Keeps the monthly savings going and replaces the pickup next year as already planned.
S0.quote: That's the thing that'd actually move us, not a chat program.
S0.fieldNote: Sam's background worry is the life of the coal mine, not technology. He is unbothered and practical, and his fallback is to drive further for the same kind of work. He doesn't follow AI news and doesn't think his workmates do either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is what it is. Mines have always changed, we went from diesel to electric shovels when I started. I'd tell the young ones to keep their heads down and keep learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be watching the trucks more than the shovel. The trucks are easy to make drive themselves, they go round and round. Shovels are harder, the face is never the same twice, so I reckon I'd be one of the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do anything big in the first year. I'd put a little more away, maybe an extra 100 a fortnight, and hold off on the new pickup. I'd keep my head down and be the best on the shovel, because the best ones get kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing there's a storm a few valleys over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell young ones to keep learning. Would you learn anything new yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'm good at what I do and I'd rather stay good at it than be average at something else. Maybe if the company made me, I'd do a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck drivers, mostly. My brother-in-law Rob drives a truck at the same mine. If the trucks go first, that's Christmas dinner with a lot of long faces.

S1.say: I'd say it is what it is, because mines have always changed, like going from diesel to electric shovels. I'd tell the young ones to keep their heads down and keep learning.
S1.think: Privately I think the trucks go first because they drive in circles, while a shovel face is never the same twice. I reckon I'd be one of the last to go.
S1.do: Puts an extra 100 a fortnight into savings and delays the new pickup. Avoids any big moves in the first year and focuses on staying the best shovel operator, though he'd do a course only if made to.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm a few valleys over.
S1.quote: I'd rather stay good at it than be average at something else.
S1.fieldNote: Sam's strategy is to be too good to cut, and he reasons that shovels are harder to automate than trucks. He wouldn't seek new skills unless pushed. His worry lands on his brother-in-law, a truck driver at the same mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not fair on people who've done everything right, but I wouldn't go marching. I'd say the government needs to sort something out for families, because no one can fix this on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I think it's bad for me. If a robot can do any work, it can dig a face, it just needs time to learn. Two years and I'd be a 45-year-old shovel man with nothing to dig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut hard straight away: no pickup, no holiday, Helen's salon fit-out on hold. Every spare dollar onto the mortgage or into the bank. I'd ask about any job on the mine that still needs a person, even if it's less money, and if there's a redundancy, I'd take it and stretch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I don't really have a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have a plan B. What's the closest thing to one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen's salon, I suppose. It's small, but people still need haircuts, I'd hope. Maybe I'd do the books and the maintenance there and we'd try to live on that and the payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much more than a bit of saving. You can't learn a trade in two years and keep the house. Two years is just time to get scared properly.

S2.say: I'd say it's not fair on people who've done everything right, but I wouldn't go marching. The government needs to sort something out for families, because no one can fix this alone.
S2.think: I think it's bad for me, because a robot that can do any work can learn to dig a face. In two years I'd be a 45-year-old shovel man with nothing to dig.
S2.do: Cuts hard straight away, dropping the pickup, the holiday and his wife's salon fit-out. Puts every spare dollar into the mortgage or the bank and asks for any remaining job on site, ready to take and stretch a redundancy.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, with no plan B.
S2.quote: Two years is just time to get scared properly.
S2.fieldNote: Sam's 'last to go' logic collapses here, and he says so plainly. He has no backup plan except his wife's small salon. He wants government help for families but wouldn't protest, which fits his middle-of-the-road views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the companies and the government should be working on it together. Not handouts forever, but help to get people into whatever's next. That's what I'd say if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be 48. I'd probably still have the shovel for three or four of them, because they'd do the trucks first. So I'd have time, but I know myself, I'd use it badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, try to get to six months of bills. I'd probably keep doing the job until the company told me something definite, then take whatever they offered. If they offered a course in maintaining the automated gear, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there every day but I can still get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the time badly. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean I'd wait. I always wait. When they brought the new shovel in I didn't touch it till they made me, and then I was the best on it in six months. I'd probably do the same here and hope there's still a six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik's fifteen and wants to be a mechanic. I'd tell him that's good, but learn the electronics side too. I'd want him to have what I haven't got.

S3.say: I'd say the companies and government should work together while there's time. Not handouts forever, but real help to get people into whatever comes next.
S3.think: I'd still have the shovel for three or four years because the trucks go first. I know myself, though, and I'd use the time badly.
S3.do: Saves harder toward six months of bills and keeps working until the company gives a definite answer. Takes any offered course on maintaining automated gear but doesn't seek one out.
S3.feel: Anxious every day, but still able to get on with things.
S3.quote: I didn't touch it till they made me, and then I was the best on it in six months.
S3.fieldNote: Sam knows his pattern is to wait and then catch up fast, and he's betting it will work again. He is candid that five years would likely be wasted by him. He wants his son to have the electronics skills he lacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people will sort it out. Mines change, towns change. I'd say let's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years puts me at 53. I'd think I can probably get most of the way to the end on the shovel. That might be wishful thinking, but it's what I'd tell myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going, honestly, and keep saving a bit more than now. If Helen wanted to grow the salon, I'd back her with some of the savings. I'd wait a few years to see how the trucks go before I did anything for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Ten years is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't waiting a risk, if it's the same end point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. But I've seen plenty of things that were coming in ten years and never came. I'd want to see the first robot shovel actually dig before I changed my whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before you acted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot shovel at a mine like ours doing a full shift on wet clay. Not a video, the real thing. If I saw that, I'd start looking the next week.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and people will sort it out. Mines change and towns change, so let's not panic.
S4.think: Privately I'd tell myself I can get most of the way to the end on the shovel at 53. That might be wishful thinking, but it's what I'd believe.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves a bit more than now. Backs his wife's salon with some savings if she wants to grow it, and waits to see a robot shovel work a full shift before making any move.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but only in the background.
S4.quote: A robot shovel at a mine like ours doing a full shift on wet clay. Not a video, the real thing.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Sam's instinct to wait wins out, and he set a very specific test for when he'd act. He names that this might be wishful thinking. His wife's salon is the family's growth plan, not his own retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have nothing ready. What would help is a decent redundancy that's guaranteed by law, and someone helping people like me find the next job instead of just a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the towns. When a mine goes, the pub goes, the football club goes, Helen's salon goes. It's not just the job, it's the whole place.

headlineQuote: When a mine goes, the pub goes, the football club goes, Helen's salon goes.
portrait: Sam Larsen is a 43-year-old senior rope shovel operator at the Granite Ridge open-cut coal mine, married to a salon owner, with two teenage kids and a mortgage. He never uses AI, worries more about the coal mine's lifespan than about computers, and believes being the best on the shovel will keep him in work. He expects trucks to be automated before shovels, but in the two-year AGI picture that logic collapses and he admits he has no plan B. With more warning he would mostly save and wait, acting only once he sees a robot shovel work a real shift.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd have nothing ready.
whatWouldHelp: A decent redundancy guaranteed by law, and a real person helping workers like him find their next job instead of just a website.
